title: ISRAEL FOUND WATER IN THE DESERT—BUT IT WAS TOO BITTER TO DRINK
paragraphs: ISRAEL FOUND WATER IN THE DESERT—BUT IT WAS TOO BITTER TO DRINK

They survived the Red Sea, escaped Pharaoh, and witnessed the impossible. But just three days later, they discovered something terrifying: Sometimes God leads you to the very place that breaks your heart before He reveals what He can heal.
“When they came to Marah, they could not drink its water because it was bitter.” — Exodus 15:23
Imagine watching the sea split open before your eyes.
Not in a dream. Not in a story someone told you. You were there.

You heard the screams of Egyptian soldiers behind you. You felt the ground trembling beneath the wheels of Pharaoh's chariots. You saw the impossible wall of water rising on either side as you walked through a place where human beings were never supposed to walk.
And when you reached the other side, you watched the waters return.
The army that had terrified your family for generations was gone.
You were free.
For the first time in your life, nobody owned you.
Nobody could whip your back.
Nobody could force your children into slavery.
You had seen what the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob could do.
And then...
Three days later, you were desperately thirsty.
No water.
No wells.
No rivers.
Nothing but heat, sand, exhaustion, and the frightening realization that freedom had brought you into a wilderness where you could die.
Then someone shouted.
“WATER!”
Imagine the relief.
Mothers grabbing their children. Fathers stumbling toward the pools. Elderly people gathering what little strength remained in their bodies.
Finally.
An answer.
A place to drink.
A reason to believe everything would be okay.
But the moment the water touched their lips...
Something was terribly wrong.
It was bitter.
Undrinkable.
And suddenly, the people who had just witnessed one of the greatest miracles in biblical history were standing beside the very thing they needed to survive...
Unable to receive it.
And here is the question that should make every believer uncomfortable: What do you do when God has brought you out of something terrible, but the place you reach next is still painful?
Because some of you know exactly what that feels like.
You prayed for the marriage to survive, but the relationship remains strained.
You begged God to open a door, but the opportunity that finally came carried difficulties you never expected.
You escaped a destructive relationship, only to discover that the wounds followed you into freedom.
You surrendered your life to Jesus, but the anxiety did not disappear overnight.
You believed God was leading you somewhere better.
And now you are standing beside your own Marah.
Looking at something you thought would satisfy you.
Wondering why it tastes so bitter.
And somewhere deep inside, where you rarely allow anyone to look, a question has been growing.
“Lord, after everything You brought me through... why am I here?”
Stay with this story.
Because what happened at Marah was not merely about water.
It was about the hearts of people learning to trust the God who had already delivered them.
And the answer God gave them points us toward a truth that reaches far beyond the wilderness.
A truth we desperately need to hear when the miracle behind us seems greater than the trouble in front of us.
Exodus 15:22 tells us that Moses led Israel away from the Red Sea into the wilderness of Shur.
They traveled three days without finding water.
Three days.
It is easy to read those words from the comfort of a chair with a glass of water nearby.
It is something entirely different to imagine thousands of people, including children and the elderly, moving through an unforgiving landscape with no dependable supply of drinking water.
Their need was real.
Their exhaustion was real.
Their fear was understandable.
Scripture does not ask us to pretend that thirst was imaginary.
But then comes the sentence that changes the entire scene.
In the original Hebrew, Exodus 15:23 reads:
וַיָּבֹאוּ מָרָתָה וְלֹא יָכְלוּ לִשְׁתֹּת מַיִם מִמָּרָה כִּי מָרִים הֵם
Vayyavo'u Maratah, velo yakhelu lishtot mayim miMarah, ki marim hem.
A close English rendering is:
“They came to Marah, but they could not drink water from Marah, because it was bitter.”
The Hebrew word מָרִים (marim) means “bitter,” while מָרָה (Marah) is the place-name associated with that bitterness.
The connection is deliberate.
The place was called Marah because of the bitterness of its water.
But notice something.
The text does not say God had abandoned them.
It does not say Pharaoh had returned.
It does not say the covenant had been canceled.
They had encountered a bitter circumstance while still traveling on the journey that followed God's deliverance.
That distinction matters.
Because too many believers interpret every painful season as proof that God has left them.
We think that if God truly loves us, the road should become easier.
If we have repented, everything should immediately improve.
If we have prayed, the answer should arrive exactly as we imagined.
If God has opened the sea, surely He will never allow us to face thirst.
But the Bible refuses to offer that kind of shallow faith.
Israel's journey teaches us that deliverance from bondage does not mean the immediate disappearance of every difficulty.
And perhaps that is where this story begins to expose something in us.
We celebrate the God who opens the sea.
But do we trust Him when the water is bitter?
We worship when the answer is yes.
But what happens when His providence leads us into a season we do not understand?
We testify when the miracle is visible.
But what happens when all we can see is another problem?
The Israelites had seen God's power.
Now they were being confronted with the question of whether they would trust His character.
Exodus 15:24 says:
“And the people murmured against Moses, saying, What shall we drink?” (KJV)
The Hebrew verb behind “murmured” is וַיִּלֹּנוּ (vayyillonu), from a verb meaning to grumble or complain.
Their question was not unreasonable.
They needed water.
But the narrative identifies their response as grumbling against Moses rather than a faithful appeal to the Lord.
And before we condemn them too quickly, perhaps we should examine ourselves.
How many times have we done something similar?
We have watched God provide before.
We have experienced mercy we did not deserve.
We have survived things that once seemed impossible.
Yet one unexpected disappointment can make us speak as though He has never been faithful.
One unanswered prayer.
One medical report.
One financial crisis.
One betrayal.
One child who walks away from the faith.
One marriage that becomes painfully quiet.
And suddenly, the memory of yesterday's mercy struggles against the weight of today's suffering.
We do not always say, “God has abandoned me.”
Sometimes it sounds more respectable.
“I just don't understand why He would allow this.”
“I've tried to do everything right.”
“I've prayed for years.”
“Maybe God hears other people, but not me.”
Sometimes those words come from genuine grief.
Sometimes they reveal a heart beginning to accuse God.
And sometimes both are tangled together so tightly that we barely know the difference.
That is why this passage deserves more than a quick religious slogan.
Because God does not respond to Marah by telling us that human pain is insignificant.
He shows us what faithful dependence looks like in the middle of genuine need.
While the people grumbled, Moses did something different.
Exodus 15:25 begins:
“And he cried unto the LORD; and the LORD shewed him a tree...”
The Hebrew says:
וַיִּצְעַק אֶל־יְהוָה
Vayyits'aq el-YHWH.
“And he cried out to the LORD.”
That word for crying out, וַיִּצְעַק (vayyits'aq), comes from a verb used for urgent calling or crying for help.
Moses did not pretend the water was sweet.
He did not deny the danger.
He did not deliver a motivational speech about positive thinking.
He cried out to God.
There is something profoundly comforting about that.
Faith does not require you to deny your suffering.
Faith brings your suffering before the One who is able to help.
There is a difference between pouring out your grief to God and allowing grief to become an accusation against Him.
The Psalms are filled with anguished prayers.
David wept.
Job lamented.
Jeremiah grieved.
Even Jesus, in Gethsemane, expressed the terrible weight of the suffering before Him while submitting Himself to the Father's will.
Biblical faith is not emotional numbness.
It is dependence.
And some of us have spent so much energy trying to appear spiritually strong that we have forgotten how to cry out honestly to the Lord.
We know how to post a Bible verse.
We know how to say, “God is good.”
We know how to smile when someone asks whether everything is okay.
But behind closed doors...
The tears come.
The questions return.
The loneliness grows.
And the heart whispers things the mouth is afraid to confess.
What if God is inviting you to stop performing strength and start seeking Him with sincerity?
Not because He does not already know your pain.
But because prayer is one of the ways He teaches His children to depend upon Him.
And then the story takes a remarkable turn.
The Lord shows Moses a tree, or piece of wood, and Moses throws it into the water.
The Hebrew of Exodus 15:25 says:
וַיּוֹרֵהוּ יְהוָה עֵץ וַיַּשְׁלֵךְ אֶל־הַמַּיִם וַיִּמְתְּקוּ הַמָּיִם
Vayyorehu YHWH ets, vayyashlekh el-hammayim, vayimtequ hammayim.
A close translation is:
“And the LORD showed him a tree; he threw it into the water, and the waters became sweet.”
Look closely at that last phrase.
וַיִּמְתְּקוּ הַמָּיִם
Vayimtequ hammayim.
“The waters became sweet.”
The verb comes from the Hebrew root מתק (m-t-q), associated with sweetness.
The water that could not be drunk became suitable for the people to drink.
But Scripture does not identify the species of tree.
It does not explain a chemical process.
It does not suggest that Moses discovered a universal natural remedy for contaminated water.
The emphasis falls on God's intervention.
The Lord showed Moses what to do.
Moses obeyed.
And the water changed.
What had been undrinkable became a provision.
What had been a source of distress became a place where God's power was revealed.
And perhaps the most striking detail is this:
God did not need to take Israel back to Egypt to provide what they needed.
He met them in the wilderness.
At the very place where their need had become undeniable.
Now, we must be careful with what we say next.
Because some sermons turn the tree at Marah into a direct prediction of the cross of Jesus Christ.
The resemblance can certainly invite Christian reflection.

Wood enters bitter water, and the water becomes sweet. Centuries later, Christ bears our sins upon the cross, and through His death and resurrection, sinners receive forgiveness and reconciliation with God.
But Exodus 15 does not explicitly identify the tree as a prophecy of Calvary.
We should not pretend it does.
The historical meaning of the passage concerns God's provision for Israel and His instruction of His redeemed people.
Yet when we read the whole Bible in light of Jesus Christ, we discover something even greater than a symbolic resemblance.
The God who provided for Israel at Marah is the God who has accomplished our redemption through His Son.
And the cross addresses a problem far deeper than bitter drinking water.
Because our greatest need is not simply for our circumstances to improve.
Our greatest need is to be reconciled to the holy God against whom we have sinned.
That is where the Gospel becomes intensely personal.
You may be able to hide your bitterness from everyone around you.
You may be able to conceal your resentment behind religious language.
You may know how to serve in church while quietly nursing unforgiveness.
You may even speak passionately about Jesus while refusing to surrender the sin you have been protecting.
But the Lord sees the heart.
He knows the anger you have rehearsed.
The envy you have justified.
The pride you have disguised as righteousness.
The secret compromises.
The prayers you stopped praying because you no longer wanted His answer to challenge your desires.
And still, the invitation of the Gospel is not to manufacture your own righteousness.
It is to repent and come to Jesus Christ.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” (KJV)
Not after we became impressive.
Not after we repaired every broken part of our lives.
Not after we earned the right to be loved.
While we were still sinners.
Christ died for us.
And 1 Peter 2:24 says of Jesus:
“Who his own self bare our sins in his own body on the tree...” (KJV)
The Greek expression includes:
ἐπὶ τὸ ξύλον
Epi to xylon.
“Upon the tree,” or “upon the wood.”
Here, the New Testament explicitly speaks of Christ bearing our sins in connection with the wood of His crucifixion.
This does not prove that the tree at Marah was a direct prophecy of the cross.
But it reminds us that the Christian's deepest hope rests not in a mysterious object placed into water, but in the crucified and risen Savior.
Jesus did not come merely to make difficult circumstances more comfortable.
He came to save sinners.
To bear our guilt.
To reconcile us to God.
To give us new life.
And that changes how we understand healing.
Because sometimes the Lord changes the circumstances around us.
Sometimes He provides an unexpected answer.
Sometimes He restores what appeared impossible to repair.
But sometimes the situation remains difficult while He works deeply within us.
The apostle Paul pleaded with the Lord concerning his thorn in the flesh.
Yet the answer he received was:
“My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness.” (2 Corinthians 12:9, KJV)
God's faithfulness is not measured by how quickly every bitter experience disappears.
And no Christian should be told that prolonged suffering automatically proves weak faith.
The cross itself destroys that assumption.
Jesus, the perfectly obedient Son of God, suffered terribly.
Yet His suffering was not evidence of the Father's abandonment of His saving purpose.
Through the death and resurrection of Christ, God accomplished redemption.
So when you stand at Marah, do not assume that pain has the final word.
But do not assume, either, that God has promised to make every earthly circumstance sweet on your timetable.
He has promised something greater to those who belong to Christ.
His presence.
His grace.
His faithfulness.
And a future in which sin, death, and suffering will not reign forever.
Revelation 21:4 speaks of the day when God will wipe away every tear, and death, sorrow, crying, and pain will be no more.
That promise is not sentimental optimism.
It is anchored in the victory of Jesus Christ.
And until that day, we learn to trust Him in the wilderness.
But there is another detail at Marah that we must not overlook.
After the waters became sweet, Exodus 15:25 says:
“There he made for them a statute and an ordinance, and there he proved them.” (KJV)
The Hebrew word associated with this testing is נִסָּהוּ (nissahu), from the root נסה (n-s-h), meaning to test or prove.
The wilderness was not merely a place where Israel needed provision.
It was also a place where their trust and obedience would be tested.
God was teaching a newly delivered people how to live in covenant dependence upon Him.
They had been rescued from slavery.
But they still needed to learn what it meant to listen to the Lord.
That should make us examine our own understanding of grace.
Because grace is not permission to remain unchanged.
The Jesus who forgives sinners also calls sinners to repentance.
The Savior who receives the broken also teaches His people to walk in holiness.
We are not saved by our obedience.
We are saved by grace through faith in Christ.
But the grace that saves us does not leave us indifferent to God's will.
Ephesians 2:8–10 holds these truths together: salvation is God's gift, not the result of our works, and believers are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
So perhaps the question at your Marah is not merely:
“When will God change this situation?”
Perhaps another question needs to be asked.
“Lord, what are You teaching me about trusting and obeying You here?”
Not every painful event is a punishment.
Not every tragedy contains a hidden lesson we can confidently identify.
We must never use the story of Marah to blame suffering people for their suffering.
But every season can become an occasion to seek the Lord faithfully.
And there are moments when hardship exposes what prosperity has allowed us to ignore.
We discover how quickly we become impatient.
How deeply we crave control.
How easily disappointment becomes resentment.
How much we have confused God's gifts with God Himself.
And perhaps that is why the story of Marah remains so unsettling.
Because the bitter water was not the only thing being revealed.
The hearts of the people were being revealed too.
Some of you are reading this while carrying a bitterness that has lasted for years.
Someone betrayed you.
Someone abandoned you.
Someone made a promise they never intended to keep.
Someone you trusted used your vulnerability against you.
You have replayed the conversation a thousand times.
You know exactly what you wish you had said.
You have imagined the apology that never came.
And even though the person may have moved on, part of your heart is still standing in that painful moment.
You are exhausted.
Not only by what happened.
But by what remembering it continues to do to you.
Listen carefully.
Forgiveness does not mean calling evil good.
It does not mean pretending abuse never happened.
It does not require returning to an unsafe relationship or removing wise boundaries.
It does not mean that justice no longer matters.
But for those who have received mercy in Christ, forgiveness becomes part of the costly journey of refusing to let vengeance rule the heart.
Ephesians 4:31–32 calls believers to put away bitterness, wrath, and malice, and to forgive one another as God in Christ has forgiven them.
That command may confront something you have been protecting.
And it may take time, prayer, wise counsel, and difficult decisions to walk it out.
But do not confuse the difficulty of obedience with the absence of God's grace.
Christ is able to sustain you while you learn to obey Him.
And perhaps today the first honest prayer is not a dramatic declaration of victory.
Perhaps it is simply:
“Jesus, I know I need to forgive, but I am still hurting. Please help me.”
That is not a glamorous prayer.
It may never receive thousands of reactions on social media.
But it can be the beginning of genuine surrender.
And there is something else.
Sometimes we are not merely wounded by what others have done.
Sometimes we are ashamed of what we ourselves have done.
That is a different kind of bitterness.
The memory of a decision you cannot undo.
The relationship you damaged.
The lie you told.
The years you wasted.
The person you became when you thought nobody was watching.
Perhaps you still attend church.
You still know the songs.
You still recognize the verses.
But whenever someone speaks about God's holiness, something inside you tightens.
Because you know.
You remember.
And you wonder whether grace can truly reach someone who knew better and sinned anyway.
If that is you, hear the Gospel.
Jesus Christ did not shed His blood only for people with respectable histories.
He came to save sinners.
Peter denied Him.
Paul had persecuted His people.
The thief beside Him had no lifetime of religious achievement to offer.
Their stories are not permission to treat sin lightly.
They are testimonies that God's mercy is greater than our ability to earn it.
First John 1:9 says:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” (KJV)
Confession is not an attempt to inform God of something He does not know.
It is the honest acknowledgment of sin before Him.
And genuine repentance turns away from sin toward the Savior.
You do not need to decorate your failure before bringing it to Jesus.
You do not need to rewrite your history to make yourself worthy.
You need the mercy of the One who died and rose again.
And if you are in Christ, your past does not have the authority to cancel what His grace has accomplished.
This is why our message at Gospel Warrior has always mattered so deeply:
Not because Jesus pretends the scandal never happened.
Not because the consequences of sin magically disappear.
Not because every broken relationship will be restored exactly as it was.
But because Christ can redeem people who cannot redeem themselves.
He can forgive real guilt.
He can give new life to real sinners.
He can teach wounded hearts to trust again.
He can take a person who once lived in rebellion and make that person a witness to His mercy.
And no failure is more powerful than the saving work of Jesus Christ.
Now return with me to the wilderness.
Return to the thirsty families.
Return to the bitter water.
Return to the moment Moses cried out.
The Lord showed him what to do.
The water became sweet.
And the people who had feared they would have nothing to drink received provision.
But the story does not end with the transformation of the water.
In Exodus 15:26, God calls Israel to listen diligently to His voice, do what is right in His sight, and heed His commandments.
Then He declares:
“For I am the LORD that healeth thee.” (KJV)
The Hebrew is:
כִּי אֲנִי יְהוָה רֹפְאֶךָ
Ki ani YHWH rof'ekha.
“For I am the LORD, your healer.”
The word רֹפְאֶךָ (rof'ekha) means “the one who heals you,” from the Hebrew verb רפא (r-f-ʾ), meaning to heal.
This declaration appears within God's covenant instruction to Israel, including a warning concerning the diseases brought upon Egypt.
It must not be twisted into a blanket guarantee that every faithful Christian will experience immediate physical healing.
Nor should it be used to accuse sick people of disobedience.
But it does reveal something essential about the Lord's character.
He is not indifferent to the condition of His people.
He is the God who provides, instructs, restores, and heals according to His wisdom and covenant purposes.
And in Jesus Christ, we see the fullest revelation of God's saving mercy.
Jesus healed the sick.
He welcomed the outcast.
He forgave sins.
He confronted hypocrisy.
He called people to repentance.
And He gave His life as a ransom for many.
The healing we need most begins with reconciliation to God.
And through Christ's resurrection, we have the hope of complete restoration in the age to come.
But there is one final detail in Israel's journey that I do not want you to miss.
It appears immediately after Marah.
Exodus 15:27 says:
“And they came to Elim, where were twelve wells of water, and threescore and ten palm trees: and they encamped there by the waters.” (KJV)
Twelve springs.
Seventy palm trees.
Water.
Shade.
Rest.
After Marah came Elim.
After the bitter water came a place where the people could camp beside abundant water.
And I can almost imagine the silence.
The children drinking without fear.
The weary sitting beneath the palms.
The families realizing they had survived another day.
The people discovering that the wilderness contained more than the bitterness they had encountered.
But we must read this faithfully.
Elim does not establish a universal promise that every Christian will receive a comfortable earthly season immediately after suffering.
The Bible contains faithful believers who endured hardship for years, and some who died without receiving earthly deliverance.
Yet Elim reminds us that Marah was not the whole story of Israel's journey.
And if you belong to Christ, your present suffering is not the whole story of your redemption either.
There is a resurrection.
There is a coming kingdom.
There is a Savior who has conquered death.
There is a future secured not by your ability to remain strong, but by the faithfulness of Jesus Christ.
So do not make permanent conclusions about God's character from a temporary view of your circumstances.
Do not let one bitter season erase the truth of the cross.
Do not let disappointment become your final theology.
And do not confuse God's silence with proof that He is absent.
He has spoken decisively in His Son.
Perhaps you are at Marah today.
Perhaps you have been there longer than anyone knows.
Perhaps your friends see the smiling photographs, but they do not see the tears after midnight.
Perhaps you have grown tired of telling people you are okay.
Perhaps your prayers have become shorter because you are afraid of hoping again.
I cannot promise that tomorrow your situation will change.
I cannot promise that the person who hurt you will apologize.
I cannot promise that the diagnosis will disappear or that the financial burden will lift.
The Bible does not authorize me to make those promises.
But I can tell you that Jesus Christ is worthy of your trust.
That His grace is sufficient.
That His mercy is real.
That His resurrection is not a metaphor.
And that everyone who comes to Him in repentant faith finds a Savior who is able to save.
If you have been running from God, come home.
If you have been hiding sin, confess it.
If you have been trusting your own righteousness, surrender it.
If you have been crushed by shame, look to the cross.
If you have been wounded by others, ask the Lord for the grace to walk in truth, wisdom, and forgiveness.
And if you are simply exhausted, cry out to Him.
Like Moses did.
Not with polished religious language.
But with an honest heart.
“Lord, I need You.”
That prayer may be the most sincere thing you have said in months.
And perhaps someone reading this needs to know that they are not the only one struggling.
You do not need to reveal private details.
You do not need to expose wounds that are not safe to share publicly.
But your simple words may remind another believer that they are not walking through the wilderness alone.
And if God has already carried you through a bitter season, consider sharing a brief testimony.
Not to make your story look impressive.
But to point someone else toward the faithfulness of Jesus.
There may be a person reading these comments who desperately needs that encouragement.
And please do not let this message end with you.
Not merely because you agree with it.
But because somewhere among your family, friends, coworkers, and acquaintances, there may be someone standing at Marah right now.
Someone whose marriage is barely holding together.
Someone whose faith has grown weak.
Someone silently grieving.
Someone who has stopped praying.
Someone who thinks their past has disqualified them from receiving mercy.
Because spiritual encouragement is not something we outgrow.
We need the Word of God when we are rejoicing.
And we need it when the water is bitter.

We want this community to be a place where believers are strengthened by Scripture, struggling Christians are encouraged to return to the Lord, seekers can encounter the truth of the Gospel, and those who have grown spiritually complacent are challenged to repent and walk faithfully with Jesus.
And for those who want to go deeper, there is another invitation.
These resources are offered freely because spiritual nourishment should never be treated as something that only paying supporters deserve to receive.
But making resources available, preparing biblical content, and continuing to reach people with the message of Jesus Christ also requires faithful support.
It is an opportunity to help sustain and expand a ministry devoted to proclaiming Christ, sharing Scripture, encouraging repentance, and helping people grow in their faith.
The New Testament teaches that Christian giving should be willing, thoughtful, and cheerful, not pressured or coerced.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” (KJV)
And Philippians 4:15–18 reminds us that believers can participate in Gospel work through material support.
That is the spirit of this invitation.
Not guilt.
Not fear.
But an opportunity to participate willingly in work you believe is faithful to the Gospel.

If Gospel Warrior has helped you return to Scripture, strengthened your faith, encouraged you through a difficult season, or pointed you toward Jesus Christ, you may wish to help make that same encouragement available to others.
These items are not the reason we proclaim the Gospel.
They are simply practical resources and reminders that can accompany a life of discipleship.
The real purpose remains unchanged.
To glorify Jesus Christ.
To make His Word known.
To encourage genuine repentance and faith.
To remind the broken that grace is real.
To help believers grow deeper in the truth.
And to reach people who may never walk through the doors of a church but may encounter a Scripture-filled message on their phone.
Read the Scriptures with us.
Pray for this work.
Encourage someone who is struggling.
Faithful service to Christ takes many forms, and the Gospel is not for sale.
What matters eternally is whether your hope rests in Jesus Christ.
And now, before you leave this story, I want you to return one last time to that scene in the wilderness.
The sun is still burning.
The desert is still vast.
The people are still far from the Promised Land.
But the water at Marah is no longer bitter.
The same place that exposed their desperate need has become a place where they have witnessed God's provision.
And they are about to continue their journey.
They do not know every trial waiting ahead.
They do not know how many times they will need mercy.
They do not know how much they still have to learn.
But the Lord has not finished dealing with His people.
And perhaps that is the word you need today.
Your story is not finished.
Not because every earthly chapter will have the ending you want.
But because, for those who belong to Christ, death itself cannot overturn the promise of resurrection.
The bitterness you are experiencing is real.
The grief is real.
The struggle is real.
But so is the cross.
So is the empty tomb.
So is the mercy of God.
And so is the invitation to trust the Savior who gave Himself for sinners.
The Israelites needed water.
We need living hope.
And Jesus says in John 7:37:
“If any man thirst, let him come unto me, and drink.” (KJV)
Do you hear the invitation?
Come to Him.
Not to a formula.
Not to a personality.
Not to a religious performance.
To Jesus.
The One who died for sinners.
The One who rose from the grave.
The One who calls the weary to Himself.
The One who can forgive what you cannot undo and give you a future you could never earn.
And when you remember Marah, remember this:
The bitter water was real. But it was never greater than the God who met His people there.
